title: The Sunstone's Secret Song
markdown:
Peregrin’s study, high among whispering cedars and cool slate roofs, always smelled of dried ink and snowmelt far below. Ravens glided on a sky so blue it felt like an ocean, their calls like pebbles dropped on a drum. Peregrin adjusted his spectacles and admired his latest acquisition: the Sunstone of Solitude. A shifty gnome merchant named Meira had assured him it amplified the mountain’s very quietness.

“A fascinating piece of… stone,” he mused, tapping its warm surface. It drank afternoon light and gave back a gentle inner gold. Pip, his owl of discerning taste, ruffled tawny feathers on a stack of tomes and offered an inquisitive hoot.

“Its potential is unexploited,” Peregrin went on, overconfident as a well-pressed sleeve. “A recalibration of resonant frequencies. Unprecedented solitude. Imagine.” He had a spell ready: captured starlight and the sighs of a sleeping wind. What could go wrong with such a judicious application?

Quite a lot, as it happened.

The final syllable left his lips and the room shivered, not with earthquake but with untamed magic. Ink in an open pot rippled. A bookmark fled. The Sunstone pulsed a frantic gold that made the tomes look suddenly underdressed. Outside, snowmelt’s peaceful murmur faltered, then surged with panicked urgency, as if every hidden stream had been told to speak at once. Pip clicked, eyes on the window, then on Peregrin, then on the window again, which was as close as an owl came to saying I told you the frequency was a bad idea.

Ravens no longer circled lazily. They wheeled and dived, anxious. Distant peaks looked restless. Ice crystals swirled with no wind to excuse them.

“A minor miscalculation,” Peregrin declared, gathering his wits as if they were dropped pins. “The Sunstone is overenthusiastic. I have upset an equilibrium. It falls to me to rectify.” He reached for the worn satchel. “We take it to the ancient Guardian of the Peaks. For that, Pip, we need a guide. A particular kind.”

He found her in the market’s cheerful chaos: barkers, dyed wool, a stall that sold only different kinds of quiet (Meira would have priced those, Peregrin thought, and sold the loudest). Elara moved like mist that had decided to be a person. Her eyes were moss after rain. A trader tried to sell her a charm against falling snow; she listened to the mountain instead and bought apples. She could hear avalanches before they began; the village treated her as a living barometer, and children asked her about weather the way other children asked about sweets.

“An escort to the Guardian?” Her voice was pine needles in summer air. “The paths are fickle. The mountain is speaking unrest.”

“Precisely why you are indispensable.” He clutched the satchel. The stone thrummed through the lining. “A balancing act.”

They left under a faded-denim sky. Cedars deepened until the path became a thought the trees were having. Resin thickened, sweet and sharp. Meltwater talked in hidden throats. Elara’s steps were sure and silent; she attended to wind, branch, tremor, the particular hush that meant snow was considering a career change. Peregrin, practised on mountains, still looked to her more often than his pride preferred. His satchel bumped his hip with the Sunstone’s too-eager heart. Pip on his shoulder hooted a warning at a bad ledge and murmured approval when Peregrin crossed loose scree without inventing a spell for it. Once, Peregrin began a flourish to dry a wet boot and stopped himself. The boot could drip. The mountain, just now, could not take another amplification.

On a windswept ridge a gust arrived sharp as a wolf’s bite. Elara froze, head tilted as if the mountain had used her name. “Avalanche.” She pushed them toward weather-beaten boulders that had survived worse conversations. Peregrin went without argument, satchel hugged, pride left on the ridge like a dropped glove. A white roar crashed past, a heartbeat from taking them, chewing the path they had meant to use. Peregrin tasted disturbed snow and the particular metal of almost. The silence after was a held breath. Ice dripped from the boulders as if counting them lucky. Pip scanned the dusted slopes with owl intensity and did not preen.

“Remarkable,” Peregrin panted. “You saved us.”

“It is the mountain speaking,” Elara said. “It warned us of its anger.”

That was the first impossible task: survive a slope that had been made impatient by solitude turned up too loud.

Later, under a sky bruised purple, they found a cave mouth hidden by ivy, lit by fireflies like fallen stars, a thin plume of cooking smoke from deeper in. The hearth was a modest animal of flame. Peregrin, pragmatic despite his sleeves, offered their dried fruit and hard bread to whoever lived there and did not ask the cave for a title. They sat. The storm practised on the ivy and failed to get in. A mountain marmot the colour of autumn leaves emerged, eyed Pip with the seriousness of a critic, and nudged a carved wooden whistle toward the owl.

“A gift!” Peregrin forgot, briefly, the satchel. “Perhaps to amplify Pip’s hoots.”

Pip blew softly. High sweet notes filled the cave. The marmot scurried out and returned with glowing moss, which it set at the entrance. The moss showed a safer path around an ice field they would have met in fading light.

Peregrin stared. “You understood it. You communicated. It helped.”

Pip hooted, which in Pip meant of course, and it was a rather charming tune.

“Inventive,” Peregrin muttered, amused despite himself. “Sometimes inconveniently so. He has solved half the problem and hidden the other half of why the mountain is restless.”

“The Sunstone,” Elara said, eyes on the satchel. “It is not only solitude. It is balance. The mountain’s heart has a thousand energies. Amplify one, and the others cry out.” She looked at Pip. “Your companion feels the connections.”

The second task had been kindness in a stranger’s cave. The third waited in stone.

They reached the Guardian’s domain the next day by the moss-lit way, Pip’s whistle now a recognized tool slung on a cord at Peregrin’s throat. The amphitheater had been carved by wind and time, walls etched with earth-stories: herds, winters, one very old argument between ice and cedar. Snow here lay quieter than the peaks they had fled. The Guardian, living stone and glacial ice, regarded them with eyes as old as the mountain’s core. Meltwater made a slow jewelry on its wrist.

“You bring the Sunstone,” it rumbled, tectonic and tired. “You disturb its peace, and the mountain’s. Your method of acquiring it was less than subtle. That gnome, Meira, I presume? Always a knack for trouble.”

Peregrin felt the foolishness land properly. “I made an error. I sought to enhance solitude and did not understand the connections. Meira, yes. Dubious.” He offered the stone. Its gold looked almost apologetic.

The Guardian’s hand was cool. “The mountain weeps for fractured harmony. Snows restless. Winds in protest.”

Pip nudged the whistle. Peregrin understood without a lecture: the little instrument was not a louder hoot. It was a way to ask.

Before he spoke, he did one unscheduled thing. He sat on a sun-warm ledge of the amphitheater and let the wind finish a sentence. Elara stood a little apart. Pip preened. Meltwater ticked somewhere in the ice of the Guardian’s shoulder. A raven crossed the open sky and did not look frantic. Peregrin counted the ticks. The stone in his lap cooled from frantic to merely warm. The mountain, if it was a beast, was not hiding. It had been speaking the whole time.

“Guardian,” he said, voice clearer. “The Sunstone amplifies what is already there. If we want harmony, we listen to the quietest voices.” He set the stone down, laid Pip’s whistle beside it, and placed a dew-kissed cedar sprig on the gold. Tiny against the amphitheater. Offered anyway.

The Sunstone pulsed with a contented warmth, a sigh instead of a shout. Restless energy receded. A breeze brought pine and damp earth.

“You cannot improve a plan,” the Guardian rumbled, and something like amusement found the stone of its voice, “without first making it significantly stranger and considerably more humble.”

Peregrin chuckled, unforced. The beast of the mountain had not needed a new shape. It had needed its volume returned.

The journey back was easier in the lungs. Ravens had gone back to being lazy commas on the blue. Peregrin did not reach for a proving spell when a stream asked to be crossed; he used the moss-path trick and his own feet. Elara’s moss-coloured eyes approved without ceremony. At the village edge she bought the same apples and did not mention avalanches, which was how he knew the mountain had stopped shouting. Pip rode his shoulder as a partner, not an ornament, and kept the whistle as if it were a second language.

The Sunstone travelled in the satchel quieter than it had left, a companion that had been asked, at last, not to shout. In the study Peregrin set it on the sill where snowmelt light could find it without being bullied. He labelled no new frequencies. He let the ink smell and the cedar smell share the room. Meira, wherever she was counting coins, would no doubt sell another wonder tomorrow. Peregrin, for once, did not want to buy it. Pip hooted once, soft, and the stone answered with nothing louder than warmth.
characters: Peregrin (overconfident wizard of the cedar peaks), Pip (discerning tawny owl), Elara (elf guide who can hear avalanches before they begin)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
